newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Swedish Riksbank sees unemployment major worry.
newsitem.headline: Swedish Riksbank sees unemployment major worry.

text.p: The governor of Sweden's central bank, Urban Backstrom, said on Thursday that Sweden's continuing high unemployment rate was worrying.
In a speech to be delivered on Thursday night, Backstrom said the country's low inflation outlook indicated there was room for long debt yields to decrease further.
He said underlying economic factors showed the crown was undervalued and should strengthen.
"A very important conclusion is that it is not possible to reach a low unemployment level in the long term by accepting a permanently high inflation rate," Backstrom said.
"In other words it is not possible to create employment in the long term by having an expansionary monetary policy.
"Most people who estimate economic trends expect unemployment to continue to be at a high level even if growth is decent in coming years."
Sweden's Labour Board on Thursday said unemployment in February was 8.4 percent.
Backstrom said the inflation outlook remained positive with the past few months showing lower consumer prices than previously.
"The inflation outlook says that there is room for a decrease in long debt yields," Backstrom said.
"Underlying economic factors say that the crown has become undervalued during weakening over the past few months and it should be able to appreciate."
He made no comment on the possible movement of interest rates, saying the bank needed more time to analyse the effects of cutting its key rate, the repo, to 4.10 percent from 8.91 percent in 1996.
"There has been large changes for example in the repo rate in the past year," Backstrom said.
"We need time to evaluate the effects of these. The picture also includes the developments on the financial markets in the past few months.
"This also necessitates that monetary policy is handled with caution."
Backstrom said he did not see it as possible for monetary policy to significantly lower unemployment, saying that instead the climate on the labour market was a key issue.
"The question is if a spirit of mutual understanding can be reached where employment is a priority when setting wages," Backstrom said.

"An important lesson seems to be that Sweden should not focus on a norm for wage setting at an average Western European level as this relatively high level can obstruct a downturn in unemployment. The model should instead be the Netherlands."
In the Netherlands, unemployment has been halved from 12 to six percent in the past ten years, partly because real wages merely have showed a moderate increase, he said.
